I've never used the fields package before, but I think it's difficult to say anything useful without knowing more about the model and research objectives?  (Folks with more expertise in this stuff could no doubt say something more precise)

- Carl

messages.subject: DRUG this week: ggplot()
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Thanks for a great first meeting of DRUG on Friday!  We have a diverse mix of users of all levels and interests, and we will learn a lot from each other.

On Friday we agreed that it would be helpful to start each Friday workshop with a ~20 minute presentation of one of these types:

1. How to do [x] in R
2. I have this project and I'm trying to do [x] in R, give me feedback on how!
3. Look at this cool thing I did in R.

This week Mike and I will be giving a quick introduction to ggplot(), an excellent tool for data exploration and producing beautiful plots. I'm collecting resources related to ggplot in this google doc: http://goo.gl/kQqIx.  If you have favorite ggplot resources or examples, please drop them in!

Next week Jacob will give a presentation on his work in R doing spatial analysis on transportation data.

I'll also compile a list of proposed topics and a sign-up for presentation in a bit. See you Friday!

Noam

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Free online course in R
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I tried out the R course at Coursera, having no background in R.

The lectures are really fast-paced and packed full of information, but there is no guided practice in how to use R. There are weekly quizes (mainly multiple choice), which were tricky but tested well the lecture material (with some of the questions requiring using R which I liked).

There are also programming assignments, and I just tried to tackle the first one of these. These assignments seem to require a lot more knowledge on R than what the lectures have provided so far. They actually were so hard that they made me give up. Quick check of the forums revealed that a lot of people had really struggled with the assignments, even with previous programming/R background.

So unfortunately I cannot recommend this course as a way to learn R from the scratch.

Cheers
Kaisa

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Free online course in R
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm thrilled this group has come together...it seems much more practical than pawing through pages and pages of frustrating forums hoping for insight!

This email is intended to start a conversation to find out how much interest there is in a workshop series or course focused on providing hands-on experience for R-beginners. It would be basic, mainly focusing on data management/manipulation - I'm envisioning that it would give new users the basic skills to navigate around a large data-set (clean, sort, etc), run basic functions (create random number series, run linear models, anovas, etc) and create useful graphics. It would provide the basic knowledge necessary to read help menus and other resources in order to learn new (more specialized) analysis techniques.

I'm curious to know a) if there is interest, and if so, b) if folks would prefer a series of workshops or a course for credit.

Thanks for the feedback!
Anna

We're looking for people to present in future weeks of our Friday work sessions.  These are informal, ~20-30 minute talks.  Let me know if you are interested.

Talks can be any of these formats:

 - "How to" - A quick introduction to a topic and pointers to more resources

 - "Here's my problem" - take the group through what you're working on and soliciting feedback

 - Best code organization practices (style guide)
 - Efficiency in coding - how to speed up your code
 - Options for coding interfaces (notepad++, RStudio...)
 - Version control (git)
 - Mixed models/GAMs
 - Bayesian stats in R
 - Spatial analytics in R
 - Genetics/bioinformatics in R
 - Population modeling
 - Producing reports with knitr/sweave
 - Modeling admixture hybridization packages...
 - MCMC and the STAN package
 - Monte Carlo simulations in R
 - Interfacing with other languages (why and when?)
 - Working with LOTS of data more efficiently
 - Cluster computing and parallel processing

I'm looking forward to a lot of interesting talks!

Noam

messages.subject: Re: GAM models
messages.body_plain:
Rosemary,

The function `AICctab` in the package `bblme` lets you compare models:

    library(bblme)
    AICctab(M1, M2, M3, M4, base = TRUE, weights = TRUE, nobs = nrow(dd))
    ##    AICc  df dAICc weight
    ## M4 -14.0 4    0.0 0.9261
    ## M1  -7.6 2    6.4 0.0374
    ## M3  -6.9 3    7.1 0.0262
    ## M2  -5.0 3    9.0 0.0103

Note that
1) M1-M4 are several different models that have been fit to the data
2) This uses AICc, not AIC, which corrects for sample size
3) `nobs` is the number of observations, in this case the number of rows in dataset `dd`
4) You get comparison of AICc, the degrees of freedom, the *deviance* (difference from the min AICc) value, and the *model weights*

The model weights give you the RELATIVE strength of the models in predicting the data.  In the example above, `M4` has 93% of the weight, so one could relatively confidently select this model as "best" of that set, and examine its parameter estimates to see if they are different from zero.  If the weights are similar between models, then its best to average models together to get a best predictor.

See Chapter 5 of Rich McElreath's book, starting around page 272, for more detail on comparing models, averaging, and getting confidence intervals for parameters when averaging models.  Link to that here: http://goo.gl/QdW2l .  To use his method, you'll need to download and install the book's R package, here: http://goo.gl/QyvWj.

> The function `AICctab` in the package `bblme` lets you compare models:
>
>     library(bblme)
>     AICctab(M1, M2, M3, M4, base = TRUE, weights = TRUE, nobs = nrow(dd))
>     ##    AICc  df dAICc weight
>     ## M4 -14.0 4    0.0 0.9261
>     ## M1  -7.6 2    6.4 0.0374
>     ## M3  -6.9 3    7.1 0.0262
>     ## M2  -5.0 3    9.0 0.0103
>
> Note that
> 1) M1-M4 are several different models that have been fit to the data
> 2) This uses AICc, not AIC, which corrects for sample size
> 3) `nobs` is the number of observations, in this case the number of rows in dataset `dd`
> 4) You get comparison of AICc, the degrees of freedom, the *deviance* (difference from the min AICc) value, and the *model weights*
>
> The model weights give you the RELATIVE strength of the models in predicting the data.  In the example above, `M4` has 93% of the weight, so one could relatively confidently select this model as "best" of that set, and examine its parameter estimates to see if they are different from zero.  If the weights are similar between models, then its best to average models together to get a best predictor.

messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: proportion of variance explained by LDA?
messages.body_plain:
hi DRUG-users,

I haven't made it to a meeting yet, but this sounds like a great group - thanks for organizing. I've hit a wall on answering a question that seems like it should be simple and I was wondering if anyone out there might have a solution?

My question is - how much of the morphological variation (10 traits) in hybrid individuals is explained by a single discriminant axis constructed from the two parental species?

First, I take standardized trait data (mean = 0, sd = 1) measured from the parental species to estimate the discriminant axis using the lda function in MASS:

data<-scale(data)
ld<-lda(species~trait1+...+trait10,data)

Second, I predict the hybrid scores on this axis using a second dataset of the same 10 standardized traits measured on hybrids:

data2<-scale(data2)
ld1<-predict(ld,newdata=data2)

To calculate the proportion of variance explained by the discriminant axis, I compare to the total variance in the hybrid dataset:

var(ld1$x[,1]) / (var(trait1+...trait10,data2)

However, this can't be right, because the proportion of variance explained by this axis is nearly double the proportion of variance explained by the first principal component of the hybrid dataset - which, by definition, should be the maximum amount of variation that any single vector can explain.

So, I think I need to rescale the discriminant axis scores back to the original trait scores? I heard that a generalized inverse matrix might be needed, but I'm not sure how. I've also tried a MANOVA-approach, which gives a rank error when using the full 16-trait dataset as response matrix.

Thanks for your help!

Chris Martin
Population Biology Graduate Group '13
fishspeciation.com <http://fishspeciation.com>
